lesson.title: Two Number Lines, One Plane: The Coordinate System
lesson.summary: Crossing two number lines at right angles creates the coordinate plane, letting every location be named by an ordered pair and letting the Pythagorean theorem measure distance between any two points.
lesson.body:
The coordinate system, also called the Cartesian plane after mathematician Rene Descartes, is built by placing two number lines at right angles to each other, crossing at a shared zero point called the origin. The horizontal number line is called the x-axis, and the vertical number line is called the y-axis. Together they let you pinpoint the exact location of any point in a flat, two-dimensional space using a pair of numbers, called an ordered pair, written (x, y), where x tells you how far to move horizontally and y tells you how far to move vertically from the origin.

To plot the point (4, -3), start at the origin, move 4 units to the right along the x-axis because the x-value is positive, then move 3 units down because the y-value is negative. The order in the pair matters enormously; (4, -3) and (-3, 4) name two completely different locations, which is why these pairs are called ordered pairs rather than just pairs. The origin itself is the point (0, 0), where both axes cross and neither coordinate moves you anywhere.

The two axes divide the plane into four regions called quadrants, numbered counterclockwise starting from the upper right using Roman numerals. Quadrant I has both coordinates positive (x > 0, y > 0). Quadrant II has a negative x and positive y. Quadrant III has both coordinates negative. Quadrant IV has a positive x and negative y. Knowing the quadrant a point lies in from its signs alone, without plotting, is a fast sanity check: the point (-5, 2) must be in Quadrant II, since x is negative and y is positive.

Worked example: find the distance between the points (1, 2) and (4, 6) using the Pythagorean relationship. The horizontal change is 4 - 1 = 3, and the vertical change is 6 - 2 = 4. These changes form the two legs of a right triangle, so the distance is the square root of (3 squared plus 4 squared), which is the square root of (9 + 16), which is the square root of 25, which equals 5. This distance formula is simply the Pythagorean theorem applied to horizontal and vertical differences, and it returns again and again once you begin graphing lines and shapes.

Locating the midpoint between two points uses a similar logic: average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates separately. The midpoint between (1, 2) and (4, 6) is ((1+4)/2, (2+6)/2), which is (2.5, 4). This point sits exactly halfway along the segment connecting the two originals, which you can verify by checking that its distance to each endpoint is equal. Midpoint and distance together give you the two most basic measurement tools available once points are placed on the coordinate plane.

The coordinate system builds directly on the number line, using two of them, one for each dimension, to convert a one-dimensional idea of location into a two-dimensional one. Everything you know about ordering, distance, and signed numbers from the number line applies separately to each axis. This plane is the stage on which nearly every graph in algebra will be drawn: equations, inequalities, and functions all become visible pictures once you can locate their solutions as points using ordered pairs.
